clinicalPearls: JET is a narrow-complex tachycardia arising from enhanced automaticity of the atrioventricular junction or proximal His bundle, characteristically with atrioventricular dissociation and a ventricular rate exceeding the atrial rate.
The postoperative form is a feared complication of paediatric cardiac surgery, especially repairs near the atrioventricular node such as ventricular septal defect and tetralogy of Fallot correction.
A rarer congenital form presents in infancy, is often incessant and can lead to tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy and carries a familial tendency.
The QRS is usually narrow and identical to sinus conduction unless rate-related aberrancy or pre-existing bundle branch block is present.
Retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction may occasionally produce 1 to 1 association, mimicking other supraventricular tachycardias and obscuring the diagnosis.
Cornerstones of postoperative management include avoiding hyperthermia, minimising catecholamines, correcting electrolytes and inducing mild hypothermia.
Because the mechanism is abnormal automaticity, direct-current cardioversion is ineffective, though atrial pacing faster than the junctional rate can restore atrioventricular synchrony.
Loss of the atrial contribution to ventricular filling makes JET poorly tolerated in the vulnerable early postoperative period.
reference.pathophysiology: JET is caused by abnormal enhanced automaticity of tissue in the atrioventricular junction or proximal His bundle, which discharges more rapidly than the sinus node and drives the ventricles independently, producing atrioventricular dissociation with a faster ventricular than atrial rate. In the postoperative setting, mechanical trauma, oedema, suture lines and stretch near the conduction system combine with high circulating catecholamines, hyperthermia and electrolyte shifts to provoke this automatic focus. The congenital form reflects an intrinsic abnormality of junctional automaticity presenting in early life. Because activation originates at or below the node, ventricular depolarisation follows the normal His-Purkinje route and the QRS remains narrow unless conduction is otherwise disturbed.
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG and rhythm strip seeking atrioventricular dissociation with ventricular rate exceeding atrial rate
atrial electrogram recording via temporary epicardial wires in the postoperative patient
continuous telemetry to monitor rate, dissociation and haemodynamic effect
serum electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium
core temperature monitoring in the postoperative period
echocardiography to assess ventricular function and structural substrate
redFlags: haemodynamic deterioration in the early postoperative period from loss of atrioventricular synchrony
incessant tachycardia leading to tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy in infants
very high junctional rates unresponsive to first-line measures
escalating inotrope and catecholamine requirement aggravating the arrhythmia
signs of low cardiac output syndrome after congenital heart surgery
reference.prognosis: Postoperative JET is usually transient and resolves within a few days with supportive measures, though it increases perioperative morbidity. The congenital form is more difficult to control and, if incessant, may cause cardiomyopathy, but responsiveness to modern rhythm control and ablation has improved outcomes.
pitfalls: Attempting direct-current cardioversion for an automatic rhythm that will not respond.
Failing to recognise atrioventricular dissociation and misclassifying JET as another supraventricular tachycardia.
Aggravating the arrhythmia with escalating catecholamines and permissive hyperthermia in the postoperative child.
Overlooking retrograde 1 to 1 conduction that masks the diagnosis.
Neglecting electrolyte correction and temperature control as primary therapeutic levers.
